lines.text: Same man. Same face. Same accent. Students rated him completely differently.
lines.headline: One trait. *Everything else.*

lines.text: In 1977, Richard Nisbett and Timothy Wilson showed students a filmed interview with one college teacher.
lines.headline: *One* teacher, *two* versions.

lines.text: Half saw him warm and friendly. Half saw him cold and strict.
Then they rated his looks, his mannerisms and his accent.
lines.headline: Now rate his ==looks.==

lines.text: Warm version? Most found his looks appealing. Cold version? Most found the exact same features irritating.
But most insisted that liking him had nothing to do with it.
lines.headline: They *didn't notice.*

lines.text: That's the halo effect. One strong impression glows over everything else.
lines.headline: The ==halo effect.==

lines.text: So when someone dazzles you, or rubs you the wrong way, judge each trait on its own.
lines.headline: One trait *at a time.*

lines.text: Save this for your next interview, on either side of the desk.

post.title: Same Teacher, Two Personalities: Students Rated His Looks Differently #shorts
post.description: The halo effect: in 1977 Richard Nisbett and Timothy Wilson showed 118 students a filmed interview with the same college teacher acting either warm or cold. Students who saw him warm mostly rated his appearance and mannerisms appealing; those who saw him cold mostly rated the very same features (and his accent) irritating, and they denied that liking him affected those ratings. Nisbett, R. E., & Wilson, T. D. (1977). The halo effect: Evidence for unconscious alteration of judgments. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 35(4), 250-256. #psychology #shorts #haloeffect #firstimpressions
